summary.text: Insects are invertebrates of the class Insecta, and they are the largest group within the arthropod phylum.
An insect has an exoskeleton, a three-part body of head, thorax and abdomen, three pairs of jointed legs, compound eyes and a pair of antennae.
With more than a million described species, insects are the most diverse group of animals and make up more than half of all animal species.

facts.label: Flight
facts.value: Only invertebrates with sustained powered flight

items.prompt: A beetle is injured, and some of its blood leaks out. Why does that not cut off its oxygen supply?

options.label: Its blood carries oxygen only to the legs and wings
It breathes through gills on its sides that work like lungs
Air reaches its tissues directly through tiny tubes, so blood does not carry oxygen
Oxygen is stored in its exoskeleton and released as needed

items.explain: Insects breathe through paired openings along their sides connected to tubes that take air directly to the tissues, so their blood does not carry oxygen.

items.prompt: A cricket keeps growing, but its hard outer covering cannot stretch. How does it get bigger?

options.label: By shedding that covering in a series of molts
By adding new layers to the covering without ever shedding
By swelling up until the covering splits for good
By stretching the covering with its jointed legs

items.explain: Growth is constrained by the inelastic exoskeleton, so development involves a series of molts.

items.prompt: A gardener finds a young insect that looks like a small adult and grows through several increasingly adult-like stages with no pupa. What kind of development is this?

options.label: Four-stage metamorphosis, with a nearly immobile pupa
Direct growth with no molts and no change of form
Development that depends on whether the insect is aquatic
Three-stage metamorphosis, through nymphal stages

items.explain: Insects with three-stage metamorphosis lack a pupa and develop through increasingly adult-like nymphal stages. Four-stage groups often have a nearly immobile pupa.

items.prompt: A male cricket rubs his wings together at dusk. What is he doing?

options.label: Releasing a scent that females can sense from far away
Making sound to attract a mate and repel other males
Flashing light to signal to other crickets
Scraping his wings clean before the next molt

items.explain: Crickets stridulate, rubbing their wings together, to attract a mate and repel other males. Moths use pheromones and lampyrid beetles use light.

items.prompt: A farmer sprays an orchard to wipe out every insect, pollinators included. What else could go wrong besides losing the pests?

options.label: Many flowering plants that depend on insect pollinators may not reproduce
The crops would be harmed by the predators of pest insects
The plants would have no way to produce flowers at all
Silkworms and honey bees would immediately take over

items.explain: Insect pollinators are essential to the reproduction of many flowering plants and so to their ecosystems, even though many insects are regarded as pests.

items.prompt: An entomologist points at an animal and says it is a true bug. Which creature does she most likely mean?

options.label: A centipede
A spider
A woodlouse
A cicada

items.explain: Entomologists reserve bugs for insects of the order Hemiptera, such as cicadas and shield bugs. Centipedes, spiders and woodlice are other terrestrial arthropods that are not insects.

paragraphs.heading: What makes an insect
paragraphs.text: Insects form the class Insecta, the largest group of arthropods. Each one has an exoskeleton and a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. It also has six jointed legs in three pairs, compound eyes and two antennae. The name comes from the Latin insectum, meaning "cut up", because an insect looks as if it has been cut into three parts.

paragraphs.heading: A huge number of species
paragraphs.text: More than a million insect species have been described, which is over half of all animal species. Estimates of the true total vary widely, but there may be some 5.5 million. The described ones make up around half of all eukaryote species, counting animals, plants and fungi. The richest orders are the true bugs, butterflies and moths, true flies, wasps, ants and bees, and beetles, and each has more than 100,000 described species.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the body
paragraphs.text: An insect's nervous system is a brain plus a nerve cord running along its belly side. It breathes through paired openings along its sides that lead into small tubes carrying air straight to the tissues. So its blood carries no oxygen, and only part of it flows in vessels. Insects see mostly with their compound eyes, helped by small ocelli, many hear with tympanal organs, and they smell with receptors, usually on the antennae and mouthparts.

paragraphs.heading: Growing up
paragraphs.text: Most insects reproduce by laying eggs. Their stiff exoskeleton does not stretch, so they grow through a series of molts. The young often differ from the adults in body, habits and habitat. Insects with four-stage metamorphosis often pass through a nearly motionless pupa, while those with three-stage metamorphosis skip the pupa and move through nymph stages that look more like the adult each time.

paragraphs.heading: Getting around
paragraphs.text: Adult insects mostly walk and fly, and some can swim. They are the only invertebrates capable of sustained powered flight, and flight evolved in them just once. Adult insects are also the only arthropods that ever grow wings, carrying up to two pairs on the thorax. Many insects spend at least part of their lives in water, with larvae that breathe through gills, and water striders can walk on the water's surface.

paragraphs.heading: Living together and signalling
paragraphs.text: Most insects live alone. Bees, ants and termites, though, are social and form big, well-organized colonies. Earwigs show maternal care, guarding their eggs and young. Insects signal to each other in many ways. Male moths detect the pheromones of females from far away, crickets rub their wings together to attract a mate and drive off rivals, and lampyrid beetles signal with light.

paragraphs.heading: Insects and people
paragraphs.text: Many insects are seen as pests by people, above all those that harm crops, and people try to control them with insecticides and other methods. Some are parasites that can spread disease. Yet insect pollinators are essential for many flowering plants to reproduce, and silkworms and honey bees were domesticated centuries ago for silk and honey. Insects are eaten on purpose in 80% of the world's nations, while human activity is seriously harming insect biodiversity.
